extracted.intended_audience: practitioners before the USPTO (patent attorneys/agents), disciplinary counsel, and attorneys facing OED proceedings
extracted.subtask_description: Standards and legal criteria governing practitioner conduct before the USPTO, evidentiary and pleading rules in USPTO disciplinary proceedings, and factors for imposing sanctions for misconduct.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prohibition on practicing in violation of another jurisdiction's rules (37 C.F.R. § 11.505)
rubrics_metrics.description: "[A] practitioner shall not practice law in a jurisdiction in violation of the regulation of the legal profession in that jurisdiction." The USPTO is considered a jurisdiction for purposes of this rule.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Court treats practice before the USPTO as governed by this rule; a suspended or excluded practitioner may not engage in practice before the Office. Violations can support disciplinary action.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of "practice before the Office" (37 C.F.R. § 11.5(b))
rubrics_metrics.description: "Practice before the Office" includes any law-related service connected with presentation to the Office relating to a client's rights under laws/regulations administered by the Office, including preparing documents in contemplation of filing, corresponding and communicating with the Office, representing a client at interviews/hearings/meetings, and advising a client concerning matters pending or contemplated to be presented before the Office.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Affirmative acts (preparing, corresponding, communicating, representing, advising) constitute practice. Mere failure to withdraw from matters, without affirmative contact, is not necessarily practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conduct prejudicial to the administration of justice (37 C.F.R. § 11.804(d))
rubrics_metrics.description: Misconduct that "impedes or subverts the process of resolving disputes" or "frustrates the fair balance of interests or 'justice' essential to litigation or other proceedings."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Unauthorized practice is treated as a serious threat to administration of justice; misconduct that undermines public confidence in the legal system can violate this rule.

rubrics_metrics.name: Division of legal fees among practitioners not in same firm (37 C.F.R. § 11.105(e))
rubrics_metrics.description: When practitioners not in the same law firm divide fees, three requirements apply: (1) the division is in proportion to the services performed by each practitioner or each assumes joint responsibility; (2) the client agrees to the arrangement, including the share each practitioner will receive, and the arrangement is confirmed in writing; (3) the total fee is reasonable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Absent written client agreement specifying the division and reasonableness, fee sharing between separate practitioners is impermissible. Evidence showing fee payments and subsequent payments to another practitioner supports violation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Obligation to keep client funds separate (37 C.F.R. § 11.115(a))
rubrics_metrics.description: Client funds shall be kept separate from the practitioner's funds; client funds must ordinarily be maintained in a separate account in the state where the practitioner's office is situated unless client consent provides otherwise.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Depositing client fees into personal or third-party accounts (e.g., spouse's account) or commingling client and personal funds violates this requirement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Handling of advanced payments — client trust account requirement (37 C.F.R. § 11.115(c))
rubrics_metrics.description: If funds involve legal fees and expenses that have been paid in advance, such monies must be deposited into a client trust account and drawn upon only when fees are earned and expenses incurred.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Putting advanced legal fees into non-trust/personal accounts (even if later used for client matters) violates this rule and creates potential harm to clients.

rubrics_metrics.name: Required records for client trust accounts (37 C.F.R. § 11.115(f)(1))
rubrics_metrics.description: Ten types of records must be kept for client accounts: (a) receipt and disbursement journals recording deposits/withdrawals with date, source, description; (b) ledger records for each separate trust client/beneficiary showing source of funds, names of persons for whom funds held, amounts, descriptions/amounts of charges/withdrawals, and names of disbursement recipients; (c) copies of retainer and compensation agreements; (d) copies of accountings to clients/third persons showing disbursements; (e) copies of bills for legal fees/expenses rendered to clients; (f) copies of records showing disbursements on behalf of clients; (g) physical or electronic equivalents of all checkbook registers, bank statements, records of deposit, pre-numbered canceled checks, and substitute checks provided by a financial institution; (h) records of all electronic transfers from client trust accounts including authorizer, date, recipient, account number confirmation, and date/time transfer completed; (i) copies of monthly trial balances and quarterly reconciliations of client trust accounts; (j) copies of portions of client files reasonably related to trust account transactions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Failure to maintain any of these records for accounts holding client funds violates the trust account rules and supports disciplinary findings. The decision lists the ten specific record types as required.

rubrics_metrics.name: Safeguards for client trust accounts (37 C.F.R. § 11.115(f)(2)-(3))
rubrics_metrics.description: Practitioner must ensure safeguards such as: only the practitioner or a person under the practitioner's direct supervision has signatory authority; withdrawals are made only by check payable to a named payee; and related controls for electronic transfers and reconciliations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Allowing a non-signatory spouse to be sole signatory or issuing checks payable to 'Petty Cash' (unnamed payee) violates these safeguards and the regulation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rules for suspended/excluded practitioners acting as paralegals (37 C.F.R. § 11.58(e))
rubrics_metrics.description: A suspended or excluded practitioner may act as a paralegal or perform services normally performed by laypersons only if: they are a salaried employee of the other practitioner or firm (or employ the other practitioner as salaried employee); they are under the supervision of the other practitioner who assumes full professional responsibility; and even then they are prohibited from communicating directly with the other practitioner's clients regarding immediate or prospective business before the Office or rendering legal advice or legal services to those clients regarding such business.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Independent-contractor relationships, separate offices, or direct client communications by the excluded practitioner do not meet these conditions and are prohibited.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pleading requirements — admission/denial of each allegation (37 C.F.R. § 11.36(c)-(d))
rubrics_metrics.description: A respondent is required to 'specifically admit or deny each allegation set forth in the complaint.' Every allegation not denied shall be deemed admitted and may be considered proven.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Vague 'insufficient knowledge' responses can be treated as admissions. Respondent's failure to investigate or request discovery before answering can lead the court to treat allegations as undisputed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evidentiary standard and admissibility in disciplinary hearings (37 C.F.R. § 11.49; § 11.50(a))
rubrics_metrics.description: The burden of proof in disciplinary proceedings is 'clear and convincing evidence.' The rules of evidence prevailing in courts of law and equity are not controlling in disciplinary hearings; hearsay is admissible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even hearsay can be sufficient to raise a genuine issue of fact; but to meet the clear-and-convincing standard, the evidence must produce a firm belief or conviction in the trier of fact.

rubrics_metrics.name: Summary judgment burdens and standards (federal summary judgment principles cited)
rubrics_metrics.description: The moving party must identify portions of the record demonstrating absence of a genuine issue of material fact (Celotex). The nonmoving party must go beyond pleadings and designate specific facts showing a genuine issue for trial; mere allegations or denials are insufficient.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Failure to produce affidavits, depositions, or other evidence to rebut documentary evidence can result in judgment as a matter of law. Courts may consider whether the nonmoving party was 'lax' in pursuing discovery when deciding whether admissions stand.

rubrics_metrics.name: Factors governing imposition of sanctions (37 C.F.R. § 11.54(b))
rubrics_metrics.description: Before sanctioning a practitioner, consider: (1) Whether the practitioner violated duties to client/public/legal system/profession; (2) Whether the practitioner acted intentionally, knowingly, or negligently; (3) The amount of actual or potential injury caused; (4) The existence of any aggravating or mitigating factors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Court applies these four-factor framework and consults ABA Standards for Imposing Lawyer Sanctions for guidance on aggravating/mitigating considerations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Examples of aggravating factors (ABA Standards referenced)
rubrics_metrics.description: Aggravating factors include prior disciplinary offenses, pattern of misconduct, multiple disciplinary violations, refusal to acknowledge wrongful nature of conduct, and substantial experience in the practice of law.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These factors increase severity of sanction. A long disciplinary history and experience making ignorance of rules less credible are cited as aggravating.

rubrics_metrics.name: Selective prosecution/ enforcement defense standard
rubrics_metrics.description: To prevail on selective enforcement, respondent must demonstrate (1) he was singled out while other similarly situated violators were left untouched; and (2) the prosecution was pursued invidiously or in bad faith (based on impermissible considerations such as race, religion, or to prevent exercise of constitutional rights).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evidence of mere selectivity without proof of invidious intent is insufficient to sustain the defense.

rubrics_metrics.name: Timing and pleading requirement for advice-of-counsel/other affirmative defenses (37 C.F.R. § 11.36(c))
rubrics_metrics.description: Special matters of defense or disability (including reliance on advice of counsel) must be identified in the respondent's answer; failure to timely plead such defenses precludes reliance on them later.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Untimely assertion of an affirmative defense is typically prejudicial to the opposing party and may be disallowed; even if timely, the defendant must provide factual support for the defense.
